blurb: A dramatic desert mustard: grey-green pinnate leaves under tall yellow plume-shaped spikes with long protruding stamens, flowering April to September on the driest, stoniest ground. It is also a selenium hyperaccumulator — striking, and genuinely not to be eaten.
water: Low; xeric — well-drained ground, little or no supplemental water once established
spread: Upright clumping from a woody base; can be short-lived
seasons: Tall yellow plume spikes April–September over grey-green foliage; dies back to a woody base in winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 9,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Dry, stony or sandy soil with sharp drainage — the Wildflower Center gives its habitat as dry, stony slopes and washes. It is also strongly associated with seleniferous shale soils, which is where its chemistry comes from.[1][3]
care.water: Low. CSU rates its moisture requirement low, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 18–24 in wide. Grey-green leaves under large plume-shaped flower spikes — CSU notes it can be short lived and wants well-drained soils.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers from spring right through to frost; CSU records the colour as yellow and the height as 2–4 ft tall.[1][3]
care.maintenance: Treat it as a short-lived but self-renewing plant: CSU notes it can be short lived, so let a little seed fall. It is a big, architectural thing at 2–4 ft, so give it space and don't crowd it. No feeding, no irrigation once established.[1][3]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

edible.summary: Do not eat. Prince's plume is a selenium hyperaccumulator that causes severe selenium poisoning in livestock.[1][3][4]
edible.caution: **Do not eat any part of this plant.** *Stanleya pinnata* is a selenium **hyperaccumulator**: it concentrates selenium to as much as 1% of its shoot dry weight, and selenium hyperaccumulators cause devastating selenium toxicity in livestock — cattle, sheep and horses — to the point that ranchers keep stock off ground where it grows. There is a historical record of the young shoots being boiled through several changes of water and eaten as a green, sometimes called 'Indian cabbage', and this guide deliberately does **not** present that as a usable preparation: the plant's selenium content depends on the soil it is growing in, cannot be judged by eye, and selenosis is serious. Grow it as an ornamental, keep grazing animals away from it, and wash your hands after handling it.[1][3][4]
